forces.title: High energy and input costs for Irish petrochemicals
forces.description: The Irish chemicals sector, including petrochemicals, faces significant margin pressure and investment uncertainty due to persistently high energy and input costs. Geopolitical disruptions in the Middle East have limited global feedstock availability, leading to volatile raw material prices linked to oil. This cost uncertainty makes margin protection a priority for businesses, potentially impacting production continuity and profitability.
forces.source_title: July 2026 Ireland Sector Snippets

forces.title: Temporary relief from Asian petrochemical import competition
forces.description: The Dutch chemical industry, including petrochemicals, experienced a temporary upturn. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz reduced Asian competition, as Asian producers faced feedstock shortages and scaled back output. This allowed European producers more room for production growth and better pricing power, leading to temporarily fuller order books and improved ability to pass on higher costs. This benefit is expected to be short-lived.
forces.source_title: Temporary uptick for Dutch chemicals masks ongoing challenges

forces.title: Global petrochemical overcapacity and cheap Asian imports
forces.description: European petrochemical producers face structural pressure from persistent global overcapacity, which has expanded by 65% in 15 years, with further growth expected, particularly from China. This leads to an inflow of cheap, often subsidized, chemical imports from Asia, intensified by the artificially low Chinese yuan. This significantly undermines the competitiveness of European producers, affecting upstream petrochemical and basic chemical segments most acutely.
forces.source_title: Temporary uptick for Dutch chemicals masks ongoing challenges

forces.title: Structurally higher European energy prices versus global rivals
forces.description: Energy prices for oil and gas in Europe remain structurally higher than in the US and China, creating a significant competitive disadvantage for European chemical producers, especially in energy-intensive petrochemicals. While the Iran war caused price increases, the underlying structural differential persists, making European production more costly and requiring substantial investment in renewable energy and greening to achieve a future-proof competitive position.
forces.source_title: Temporary uptick for Dutch chemicals masks ongoing challenges

forces.title: Rising CO2 costs and mandates for greening petrochemical production
forces.description: European chemical producers, including petrochemicals, face increasing CO2 costs and pressure to step up electrification and adopt bio-based feedstocks. While the EU Commission aims to provide leeway on ETS rules, faster greening and reduction of fossil fuels and feedstocks are essential for long-term competitiveness. These costs add to the operational burden, especially for hard-to-abate sectors like petrochemicals, impacting their profitability and investment decisions.
forces.source_title: Temporary uptick for Dutch chemicals masks ongoing challenges

forces.title: Limited CBAM protection for most petrochemical products
forces.description: The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) currently does not cover most petrochemical products, only fertilisers, cement, aluminium, iron, steel, hydrogen, and electricity. This leaves producers of hard-to-abate petrochemicals vulnerable, without protection against carbon-intensive imports, as free emission allowances under the ETS are phased out. This exposes European petrochemical producers to a competitive disadvantage against non-EU imports with lower carbon costs.
forces.source_title: Temporary uptick for Dutch chemicals masks ongoing challenges

forces.title: Dutch government support for basic industry competitiveness
forces.description: The Dutch government is implementing policies to improve competitiveness for basic industry, including petrochemicals. This involves reintroducing the Indirect Cost Compensation scheme for large electricity consumers for three years, aiming to dampen high Dutch electricity costs. Additionally, plans to further reduce electricity costs from 2028 and abolish the national CO2 levy could support recovery in chemical plant utilisation and narrow the cost gap with neighboring countries.
forces.source_title: Temporary uptick for Dutch chemicals masks ongoing challenges

forces.title: Lagging financial performance and low capacity utilization in European chemicals
forces.description: The European chemicals industry, including petrochemicals, is experiencing a structural decline in performance. European chemical companies have shown negative total shareholder returns and underperformed broader markets between December 2022 and December 2025. In 2025, EU chemical capacity utilization was significantly below the long-term average, leading to a sixfold increase in plant closures since 2022, representing a 9 percent loss of regional production capacity.
forces.source_title: A dual transformation agenda for Europe’s chemicals industry

forces.title: Intensified global competition from low-cost Chinese producers
forces.description: European petrochemicals face severe pressure from intensified global competition, particularly from Chinese players. Chinese companies have substantially expanded their capacity and achieved cost positions that are difficult for European producers to match. Furthermore, China is rapidly closing the technological gap and accelerating product innovation, making it challenging for European companies to maintain their competitive edge in the global market, leading to market share erosion.
forces.source_title: A dual transformation agenda for Europe’s chemicals industry

forces.title: European economic downturn impacting key customer industries
forces.description: Europe’s broader economic downturn negatively affects major chemical customer industries, such as automotives. This downturn, combined with a trend of production increasingly shifting away from Europe, reduces demand for petrochemical products. This decline in demand from key end-use sectors contributes to the structural challenges faced by European chemical companies, dampening their growth prospects and profitability across the region.
forces.source_title: A dual transformation agenda for Europe’s chemicals industry

forces.title: Global shift to ethane-based polyethylene production
forces.description: The global polyethylene (PE) market is witnessing a structural shift towards ethane-based production, primarily in regions like the US Gulf Coast and the Middle East where ethane feedstock is abundant and cheaper. This trend inherently disadvantages European PE producers, whose operations are predominantly naphtha-based, making them less competitive due to higher raw material costs and greater by-product dependency in the global market.
forces.source_title: Polyethylene: Widely produced—but not one-size-fits-all

forces.title: Declining naphtha supply from reduced oil refining for petrochemicals
forces.description: A key risk for European petrochemicals is the potential decline in naphtha supply. As electrified transportation increases, oil refining operations could be reduced, consequently constraining the availability of naphtha. This feedstock is crucial for naphtha cracking, which produces essential petrochemical byproducts like aromatics (benzene, toluene, xylenes), impacting the broader petrochemical ecosystem that relies on a diversified feedstock mix and potentially driving up costs for European producers.
forces.source_title: Polyethylene: Widely produced—but not one-size-fits-all

forces.title: Projected phase-out of European ethylene capacity due to high costs
forces.description: Europe is facing an anticipated phase-out of up to five million tons per year of existing ethylene plant capacity over the next five years. This structural headwind is driven by weaker feedstock competitiveness for naphtha-based crackers, higher capital costs for plant upgrades, prolonged and unpredictable permitting timelines, and increasing regulatory and societal constraints specifically targeting plastics production, making European operations less viable.
forces.source_title: Polyethylene: Widely produced—but not one-size-fits-all

forces.title: High raw material and utility costs for German polyethylene production
forces.description: European polyethylene (PE) producers, particularly those in Germany, face significantly higher raw material and utility costs compared to ethane-based regions like Saudi Arabia and the US. Naphtha, being globally traded and typically more expensive than locally priced ethane, accounts for the main cost variation. Additionally, higher energy consumption in integrated naphtha-based plants, coupled with reliance on imported or globally priced energy, amplifies this cost disadvantage.
forces.source_title: Polyethylene: Widely produced—but not one-size-fits-all

forces.title: Higher capital expenditures for naphtha cracking in Germany
forces.description: European polyethylene producers, relying on naphtha cracking technology, face materially higher capital expenditures compared to ethane cracking facilities. For example, Germany's capital expenditures are $475 per ton of PE, significantly higher than the $290 per ton in the United States. This is due to the greater complexity of equipment required for naphtha cracking, contributing to the overall cost disadvantage for new investments and limiting modernization.
forces.source_title: Polyethylene: Widely produced—but not one-size-fits-all

forces.title: Weak internal rates of return on German polyethylene investments
forces.description: New polyethylene investments in European regions like Germany show weak internal rates of return (IRR), estimated close to the 8 percent discount rate, despite higher regional selling prices. This contrasts sharply with ethane-advantaged regions offering 10-15 percent IRRs. These subdued financial returns act as a significant disincentive for private investors, thereby limiting new capacity additions and modernization efforts in the German PE sector.
forces.source_title: Polyethylene: Widely produced—but not one-size-fits-all

forces.title: Shift to importing ethylene for downstream PE production
forces.description: European operators are increasingly opting not to reinvest in their existing ethylene crackers due to economic disadvantages. Instead, there is a structural shift towards running downstream polyethylene (PE) assets using imported ethylene. This signals a move away from fully integrated production models towards more flexible supply chain approaches, recognizing the cost-competitiveness of imported feedstocks over domestic cracker operations and impacting investment in European cracker capacity.
forces.source_title: Polyethylene: Widely produced—but not one-size-fits-all

forces.title: Opportunity for differentiated, sustainable plastics in Europe
forces.description: European polyethylene manufacturers have an opportunity to pivot from competing solely on cost in commodity PE to developing higher-value, differentiated plastics. This involves focusing on products with improved performance for specific applications or those incorporating recycled content or lower emissions. This strategic shift allows manufacturers to create market segments where competition is based on sustainability and innovation, rather than just raw material cost, improving margin potential.
forces.source_title: Polyethylene: Widely produced—but not one-size-fits-all

forces.title: Policy-driven demand for sustainable plastics materials
forces.description: Policymakers in higher-cost regions like Europe can create demand for specific types of polyethylene (PE) through mandates. Demand mandates, such as recycled content requirements, and waste regulations like restrictions on landfills or incineration, increase the supply and use of recycled plastics. Carbon pricing and border adjustments can further raise the cost of emissions-intensive production, steering demand towards sustainable and differentiated PE products, creating new market opportunities.
forces.source_title: Polyethylene: Widely produced—but not one-size-fits-all

forces.title: Mandatory recyclability under new EU Packaging and Waste Regulation
forces.description: The new EU Packaging and Waste Regulation, effective August 2026, introduces mandatory recyclability requirements for all packaging within the EU. This represents a significant structural change for the plastics and packaging industry, including polymer producers, as it necessitates a fundamental shift in product design, material choices, and recycling infrastructure to meet the stricter environmental compliance standards across the value chain, impacting materials specification and demand.
forces.source_title: Bank of Ireland Sectors Team — Developments & Insights May 2026

forces.title: Higher petrochemical feedstock costs from Middle East conflict
forces.description: Petrochemicals & polymers are highly exposed to increased feedstock costs stemming from the Middle East conflict. This geopolitical disruption leads to price spikes in oil and gas and creates supply chain risks around critical choke points like the Strait of Hormuz. For a sector that accounts for a significant portion of global plastics and resins supply, these elevated input costs directly impact manufacturing profitability for packaging, automotive, and consumer goods, causing widespread supply chain disruption.
forces.source_title: Bank of Ireland Sectors Team — Developments & Insights May 2026

forces.title: Sustained global demand for petrochemical feedstocks
forces.description: Despite the flattening demand for road fuels due to electric vehicles, global oil demand is projected to hold primarily due to continued and significant need for petrochemical feedstocks. Bain forecasts that petrochemical feedstocks will account for 16 to 19 million barrels per day of oil demand by 2040, underpinning the long-term relevance and demand for the petrochemicals sector globally, including European producers, providing a fundamental demand base.
forces.source_title: Global Energy and Materials Outlook 2026

viewpoints.title: Irish chemical sector profitability declines due to high energy and feedstock costs
viewpoints.description: Allianz_ie expresses a negative outlook for the Irish chemicals sector, including petrochemicals, anticipating declining profitability. This is primarily attributed to persistently high energy and input costs, exacerbated by Middle East logistics disruptions that limit feedstock availability globally. The volatility of oil-linked raw material prices creates significant cost uncertainty, further pressuring margins and impacting investment confidence across the industry.

viewpoints.title: Dutch petrochemicals temporarily benefit from reduced Asian competition and stockpiling
viewpoints.description: ING_Think observes a cautious_positive, but temporary, improvement in the Dutch chemical industry's outlook, specifically benefiting petrochemical producers. The initial closure of the Strait of Hormuz reduced competition from Asian producers, who faced feedstock shortages and scaled back output. This, coupled with precautionary inventory building by customers, allowed Dutch producers more room for production growth and better pricing power, despite the overall subdued long-term outlook.
viewpoints.source_title: Temporary uptick for Dutch chemicals masks ongoing challenges

viewpoints.title: European petrochemicals face structural pressure from overcapacity and cheap imports
viewpoints.description: ING_Think holds a cautious_negative long-term view for European petrochemical producers, including those in the Netherlands. The sector faces significant structural challenges from global overcapacity, notably a 65% expansion over 15 years, with continued growth expected, particularly from China. This leads to an inflow of cheap, often subsidized, chemical imports from Asia, intensified by the artificially low Chinese yuan and US import tariffs, severely pressing European margins.
viewpoints.source_title: Temporary uptick for Dutch chemicals masks ongoing challenges

viewpoints.title: European chemicals sector suffering from persistent underperformance and capacity closures
viewpoints.description: McKinsey notes a negative structural trend for the broader European chemicals industry, which includes petrochemicals. The sector experienced negative total shareholder returns from December 2022 to December 2025, underperforming wider markets. Capacity utilization in the EU was approximately seven percentage points below its long-term average in 2025, leading to a sixfold increase in plant closures since 2022, resulting in a 9 percent loss of regional production capacity.
viewpoints.source_title: A dual transformation agenda for Europe’s chemicals industry

viewpoints.title: European PE investment declines amid high costs and regulatory constraints
viewpoints.description: McKinsey presents a negative outlook for polyethylene (PE) investment and capacity in Europe. The region faces a projected phase-out of up to five million tons of yearly ethylene plant capacity over the next five years. This decline is attributed to a combination of factors including weaker feedstock competitiveness compared to ethane-based regions, higher capital costs for naphtha cracking, longer and less predictable permitting timelines, and increasing regulatory and societal constraints on plastics.

demand_drivers.description: Rising global population, particularly in emerging markets, contributes to increased demand for consumer goods and packaging, which extensively use PE.
Growing urbanization in emerging economies leads to increased construction activity and infrastructure development, boosting demand for PE in applications like pipes and other construction materials.
Expanding consumer markets, especially in emerging economies, drive demand for packaged foods, medical devices, and industrial products, all of which are significant end-uses for PE.

market_sizing.methodology: Global installed capacity for polyethylene (PE) currently stands at roughly 150 million metric tons per year. Long-term scenarios forecast annual demand growth to rebound to about 3%, reaching 200 million tons annually by 2035, primarily driven by demand in emerging markets. In recent years, growth in the industry has slowed to approximately 1 to 2 percent per year.

McKinsey analysis indicates that up to five million tons of yearly capacity of existing European ethylene plants could be phased out over the next five years. This projection reflects challenges such as weaker feedstock competitiveness, higher capital costs, unpredictable permitting timelines, and growing regulatory and societal constraints on plastics.

demand_drivers.description: Persistent global industrial production and manufacturing processes require a steady and substantial supply of petrochemicals as fundamental building blocks for various goods.

market_sizing.methodology: Bain's Global Energy and Materials Outlook forecasts that global oil demand will be significantly supported by petrochemical feedstocks. By 2040, petrochemical feedstocks are projected to account for 16 to 19 million barrels per day (Mb/d) of oil demand, playing a crucial role in maintaining overall oil consumption despite the rise of electric vehicles.
